questions.q: According to Thomson's plum pudding model, how is the atom described?
options: A tiny dense positive nucleus orbited by electrons at relatively large distances
A positively charged fluid with negatively charged electrons scattered throughout, like plums in a plum pudding
Equal numbers of protons and neutrons packed into a central core with no electrons
A cloud of negatively charged fluid with positive particles strewn through it
questions.explanation: Thomson proposed that the atom consists of a positively charged fluid with his negatively charged electrons scattered throughout, the electrons strewn through the positive body just as plums are in a plum pudding. The model was untested for how the positive charge was actually arranged, which is exactly where the gold foil experiment later attacked it.

questions.q: In Marsden's experiment with thin gold foil, what fraction of the alpha particles were deflected by angles greater than 90 degrees, with some reflected back in the direction from which they had come?
options: About 1 in 80 particles
About 1 in 800 particles
About 1 in 8000 particles
About half of all the particles
questions.explanation: Most alpha particles fired at the thin gold foil were deflected only a small amount (if at all), but a very small fraction, about 1 in 8000 particles, were deflected by angles greater than 90 degrees, some reflected straight back. Rutherford called this as incredible as firing a fifteen-inch shell at tissue paper and having it come back at you.

questions.q: Most alpha particles passed through the empty regions of the atoms far from the nucleus and were deflected from their paths by only a small amount. What does this observation indicate about the atom?
options: The atom is mostly empty space, with the deflecting charge concentrated in a tiny central region
The positive charge is spread uniformly throughout the whole atom
The alpha particles are attracted toward the negative electrons
The atom contains no positive charge at all
questions.explanation: When the alpha particles passed through the empty regions of the atoms far from the nucleus they were deflected by only a small amount; the closer to the nucleus their path was, the greater the electrostatic repulsion and the greater the deflection. The fact that almost all sail through shows the atom is overwhelmingly empty space.

questions.q: From memory, recall the three observations of the gold foil experiment ('Through, Turned, Thrown back') and the specific property of the atom each one proves.
keyPoints: Through: most alpha particles pass straight through with little or no deflection, proving the atom is mostly empty space and the deflecting core is tiny.
Turned: a small fraction are deflected through large angles by electrostatic repulsion, proving the positive charge is concentrated in a small central region.
Thrown back: about 1 in 8000 are deflected by more than 90 degrees, proving that central region is also dense and holds almost all the atom's mass.
questions.explanation: If you separated all three observations and paired each to its own property (empty, charged, massive), grade Good or Easy. Lumping them into 'some bounced back so there's a nucleus' collapses three marks into one.

questions.q: In Rutherford's nuclear model, electrons orbited around the outside of a much more massive positive nucleus much as the planets orbit the sun. What fraction of the atom's overall mass did this nucleus contain?
options: About 1 percent
About 50 percent
About 99.9 percent
Exactly 100 percent, leaving the electrons massless
questions.explanation: Rutherford proposed a nuclear atom in which electrons orbited the outside of a much more massive positive centre or nucleus, much as the planets orbit the sun, which is why it is also called the planetary model. This large nucleus contained 99.9 percent of the atom's overall mass.

questions.q: According to Maxwell's theories of electromagnetism, why would electrons in orbit around the nucleus lose energy and spiral into the nucleus?
options: Because the electrons collide with air molecules inside the atom
Because orbiting electrons are accelerating charges, so they emit electromagnetic radiation and thereby lose energy
Because the positive nucleus attracts the electrons by gravity
Because the electrons gain energy until the orbit becomes too large
questions.explanation: If electrons are in orbit around the nucleus they are accelerating, and according to Maxwell's theories of electromagnetism an accelerating charge emits electromagnetic radiation. In giving off this radiation the electrons lose energy and their orbits deteriorate until they spiral into the positive nucleus, predicting that atoms should be unstable.

questions.q: State the two main shortcomings (limitations) of Rutherford's model of the atom regarding the radiation emitted and the stability of atoms.
keyPoints: As an electron spiralled in and orbited faster, the frequency of the radiation given off would become increasingly larger, predicting a continuous spectrum; but atoms emit characteristic spectral lines instead.
The model implied atoms would be unstable as electrons spiral into the nucleus; in reality the general stability of matter shows atoms are very stable.
Both failures (the spectrum and the stability) trace back to the accelerating orbiting electron radiating electromagnetic energy, by Maxwell.
questions.explanation: Remember the two S's: Stability and Spectrum. If you recalled the rising frequency/continuous-spectrum failure AND the instability failure, both rooted in Maxwell, grade Good or Easy.

questions.q: The radius of a hydrogen atom is about 2.1 x 10^-11 m and the radius of its proton nucleus is about 0.85 x 10^-15 m. Calculate the ratio of the radius of the atom to the radius of its nucleus.
questions.explanation: The atom's radius is roughly 2.5 x 10^4 times the radius of its nucleus, showing the atom is overwhelmingly empty space. If a laboratory 10 m across represented the atom, the nucleus would be only about 0.4 mm in diameter.

questions.q: An alpha particle is a helium nucleus carrying a charge of +2e. Taking the elementary charge as 1.6 x 10^-19 C, calculate the charge on an alpha particle.
questions.explanation: The alpha particle is a helium nucleus of two protons and two neutrons, so it carries +2e, about +3.2 x 10^-19 C. Being positive, heavy and fast is exactly what lets its electrostatic repulsion from the positive nucleus do all the work in the scattering argument.

questions.q: Describe the role of the gold foil, the evacuated apparatus and the movable scintillation screen in the 1911 apparatus used to study alpha particle scattering. (3 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: The metal foil used was gold because it can be hammered extremely thin, only a few hundred atoms thick, so alpha particles pass through a thin layer of atoms and the scattering can be studied cleanly. The apparatus was evacuated so that the alpha particles are not scattered by air molecules, meaning any deflection can be attributed to the gold atoms alone. Polonium was the alpha particle source, and the microscope and scintillation screen could be rotated to observe the alpha particles at different angles, allowing the number scattered at each angle (including the rare large-angle deflections) to be counted.

criteria.descriptor: Gold foil is the thin target (a few hundred atoms thick) so alphas pass through a thin layer of atoms.
The evacuated apparatus removes air so deflection is due to the gold atoms, not air molecules.
The scintillation screen and microscope can be rotated to count alpha particles scattered at different angles.

questions.explanation: Each component is in the apparatus for a reason: gold for thinness, vacuum to isolate the gold's effect, and the rotating screen to catch the rare large-angle scattering that was the key result.
